chapters.title: The theme in one minute
chapters.readings: Stam & van de Ven 2021, p. 811; Spigel & Harrison 2018, p. 161
paragraphs: In plain words, an entrepreneurial ecosystem is the local setting that makes it easier or harder to start a firm. It is the money, the mentors, the skills and the culture around a founder.

Stam and van de Ven, 2021, take their definition from Hawley. An ecosystem is marked by co-evolution, mutualistic interdependence and diverse, nested actors. The idea comes from biology, and it keeps three features. The parts change together, they depend on each other, and they sit inside larger systems.

Spigel and Harrison, 2018, add a distinction that is easy to remember. An ecosystem has munificence, which is how many resources it holds, and functionality, which is how easily an entrepreneur can reach them. A rich ecosystem with blocked access is not the same as a rich one with open doors.

Why does the course care? Because the exam may ask how an ecosystem promotes or inhibits sustainable transformation. You need a way to say what an ecosystem is made of, and then a way to say what it does.
Remember: resources, access to those resources, and the setting that holds them together.

checks.q: What are the two dimensions Spigel and Harrison separate?
checks.a: Munificence, how many resources an ecosystem holds, and functionality, how easily they can be reached.

checks.q: What three features does the biological definition keep?
checks.a: Co-evolution, mutualistic interdependence and diverse, nested actors.

chapters.title: The key ideas
chapters.readings: Spigel & Harrison 2018, pp. 158, 159; Autio et al. 2014, p. 1100
paragraphs: Four ideas carry the theme.

The first is that an ecosystem is a process, not a thing. Spigel and Harrison, 2018, say it is better understood as an ongoing process through which entrepreneurs acquire resources, knowledge and support. That sentence is worth learning, because it turns a list into a flow.

The second is that access matters more than presence. The same authors argue that firms which can reach the resources will be more competitive, and that access depends on an entrepreneur's perceived legitimacy. Two founders in the same city can face different ecosystems.

The third is recycling. Successful founders come back as investors and mentors, and workers from failed ventures carry their skills elsewhere. Recycling depends on a culture that does not punish failure.

The fourth comes from Autio and colleagues, 2014. Context works in two ways. Selection effects decide who becomes an entrepreneur, through opportunity costs and social legitimacy. Strategic choice effects decide what those who enter then judge desirable and feasible.

There is a fifth idea that the lecture adds. An ecosystem can be built on purpose. A house that gathers capital, mentors and firms is an attempt to raise functionality, and not only munificence. That is why the policy list in Class 4 matters: it names the levers a region can pull, from arenas to risk capital to immigration.
Remember: a process, access over presence, recycling, and a context that selects and shapes.

checks.q: What does an entrepreneur need besides resources being present?
checks.a: Access to them, which depends on perceived legitimacy.
Opportunity costs and social legitimacy decide who becomes an entrepreneur.

chapters.title: The model, step by step
chapters.readings: Stam & van de Ven 2021, p. 813; Spigel & Harrison 2018, p. 163
paragraphs: There are two models to know.

The first is the ten elements in three groups. Stam and van de Ven, 2021, organise the ecosystem like this. First, the institutional arrangements, which are formal institutions, culture and networks. Second, the resources, which are infrastructure, finance, leadership, talent, knowledge, intermediate services and demand. Third, the output, which is productive entrepreneurship.

The second is the four ecosystem types. Spigel and Harrison, 2018, place ecosystems on two axes, resources and networks. First, the strong type, with many resources and well functioning networks, as in Silicon Valley. Second, the arid type, with sparse resources but working networks, as in some developing economies. Third, the irrigated type, with many resources and poor networks. Fourth, the weak type, with sparse resources and poor networks, as in deindustrialised regions.

The two models answer different questions. The ten elements tell you what to look at. The four types tell you what combination you are looking at. In an exam, name the model you are using. A list of elements and a typology of systems are different tools, and mixing them without a word of explanation costs marks.
Remember: ten elements in three groups, and four types on two axes.

checks.q: What are the three groups of elements?

checks.a: Many resources and poorly functioning networks.

chapters.title: Norway examples
paragraphs: The Norwegian examples come from the lecture rather than from the papers.

The first is an investor and founder house in Bergen, at Jahnebakken. Class 4 presents it as a local case of an ecosystem being built, where capital, mentors and new firms are gathered in one house. Read it with the ten elements, and you can see which ones the house tries to strengthen.

The second is policy. Class 4 lists the ways public policy can support an entrepreneurial community, and one of them is immigration policy. Norway uses work visas as one lever for entrepreneurs, beside start-up visas in other countries.

Use the examples carefully. The papers do not study Norway, so the Norwegian material illustrates the concepts rather than proving them. Say that in an answer, and you show that you know the difference between a case and a finding.
Remember: Jahnebakken in Bergen, and work visas as a policy lever.

checks.q: What does the Jahnebakken case show?
checks.a: A local attempt to gather capital, mentors and new firms in one house.

checks.q: Why should you mark the Norwegian material as illustration?
checks.a: Because the papers do not study Norway, so it illustrates rather than proves.

chapters.title: How the exam asks about it
chapters.readings: Autio et al. 2014, p. 1100; Stam & van de Ven 2021, p. 827
paragraphs: The practice question for this theme asks how an entrepreneurial ecosystem can promote or inhibit sustainable transformation, with examples.

Here is the shape of a good answer. Define the ecosystem with Hawley, and name munificence and functionality. Then bring in the ten elements, grouped as institutions, resources and output. Then use selection and strategic choice to explain how context shapes what founders attempt. Add the Norwegian illustration, and mark it as an illustration.

Then answer the question directly. An ecosystem promotes transformation when it holds resources that green ventures need and lets founders reach them. It inhibits transformation when the resources exist but access depends on a few gatekeepers, or when legitimacy is given only to familiar kinds of venture.

One caution from Stam and van de Ven, 2021. Their index explains a good part of the variation in high growth firms, and they still call the tests indications of tendencies rather than proof. Use the same care in your own sentences.
Remember: define, group the elements, explain the context, illustrate, and answer both sides.

checks.q: How do you answer both sides of the practice question?
checks.a: An ecosystem promotes when resources are rich and reachable, and inhibits when access depends on a few gatekeepers.

checks.q: How careful are the authors about their own index?
checks.a: They call the tests indications of tendencies, not causal proof.

chapters.title: Test yourself
chapters.readings: Spigel & Harrison 2018, pp. 160, 164; Stam & van de Ven 2021, p. 813
paragraphs: Question one. What is the difference between munificence and functionality?
Pause the audio and answer in your head.
Here is the answer. Munificence is how many resources an ecosystem holds. Functionality is how easily an entrepreneur can reach them. A rich ecosystem can still be hard to use.
Question two. Why does access matter more than presence?
Pause the audio and answer in your head.
Here is the answer. Because a resource that a founder cannot reach does not help that founder. Access depends on perceived legitimacy and on the networks a person can use.
Question three. What is recycling, and what does it depend on?
Pause the audio and answer in your head.

Here is the answer. It is the return of successful founders as investors and mentors, and the movement of workers from failed ventures into new ones. It depends on a culture that does not punish failure.
Remember: resources, access, recycling and context, and a Norwegian illustration that stays an illustration.

checks.q: What does a founder house try to raise?
checks.a: Functionality, the ease of reaching resources, and not only their number.

checks.q: Which policy lever does Class 4 link to Norway?
